lesson.title: Never Again: Why America Turned Inward Before World War Two
lesson.summary: Scarred by the costs of World War One and disillusioned by its aftermath, many Americans in the 1920s and 1930s believed the nation should stay out of Europe's conflicts, a mood that shaped US policy right up until Pearl Harbor.
lesson.body:
American reluctance to engage with Europe's problems had deep roots. The Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles and join the League of Nations in 1919 and again in 1920, largely due to opposition led by Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, who worried the League would drag the United States into future foreign wars without full congressional control. This early rejection set a tone of avoiding permanent international commitments that persisted for two decades.

That skepticism deepened over time. Many Americans came to believe that World War One had been fought less for any real national interest and more for the benefit of bankers and arms manufacturers. Senator Gerald Nye chaired Senate hearings from 1934 to 1936 investigating whether arms makers and financiers had helped push the United States into World War One for profit, and the findings reinforced a popular narrative of wartime profiteers, sometimes called merchants of death, that made the public even more wary of overseas involvement.

This mood persisted even as fascism grew more aggressive across Europe through the 1930s. Many isolationists argued that Europe's conflicts were not America's responsibility to solve, and that the Atlantic and Pacific oceans offered natural protection from foreign threats.

Organized isolationism reached its peak with groups like the America First Committee, founded in 1940, whose prominent public voices included the famous aviator Charles Lindbergh. These groups argued strongly against American involvement even after war had already broken out in Europe. This deeply held isolationist sentiment shaped legislation such as the Neutrality Acts and limited how far Roosevelt could push aid to Britain and France, a constraint that only fully broke down after the attack on Pearl Harbor.
